mqlite benchmarks, sizing & tuning

Measured, reproducible numbers for the mqlite engine across realistic workloads — not a single throughput figure — plus what they mean for deployment sizing and tuning. The suite exercises throughput, write amplification, whole-process memory and reclamation, DB-file bloat vs reclamation, KV-property (enriched) messages, a body-size sweep, and load ramp / consumer churn. Run locally (a fast multi-core box) and on a deliberately tiny cloud box so the two tell different truths.

Philosophy: measure before claiming. Each result below names its harness and environment; committed harnesses include test/bench/ and native Go benchmarks. These are historical workload measurements, not capacity guarantees for any release. Recheck the current binary with your message sizes, concurrency, queue count and monitoring load before selecting a memory or CPU limit.

Sizing & deployment (Fly.io)

The historical sample below ran a single broker on a 256 MB Fly machine. Treat these measurements as starting points for a workload-specific sizing test; they do not establish a safe backlog threshold or the current release image size.

Topology: mqlite is single-writer: run one broker or embedded Engine per database. A local process holds a file lock, so run one machine per volume and do not horizontally scale several machines onto the same SQLite file. Turso/libSQL provides managed remote storage, but it does not make overlapping brokers safe; see turso.md.

Peak backlog depth is a primary disk-sizing input, rather than lifetime throughput (Complete/Purge delete rows). Also budget for WAL growth, SQLite page and index overhead, reclamation lag, readers that delay checkpoints, and backups. Background incremental_vacuum returns freed pages to the OS over time (see §3), but does not make the backlog estimate a hard file-size ceiling:

backlog depth (256 B msgs) DB on disk Fly volume
100k ~40 MB 1 GB
1M ~0.4 GB 1 GB
5M ~2 GB 3 GB

Environments

Local (baseline) Cloud (constrained)
Where Docker (run-bench.sh) on the dev machine Fly.io app mqlite-bench, region sin
CPU 12 vCPU, arm64 (Apple Silicon, linuxkit VM) shared-cpu-1x → GOMAXPROCS=1 (a fraction of one amd64 core, CPU-steal)
Memory 8 GB 256 MB (≈207 MB usable)
Disk overlayfs in the Docker VM machine rootfs overlayfs (no volume mounted for the bench)
Probe /proc/self/{io,stat} + 200 ms RSS/heap/file sampler same binary, same matrix

Honesty notes: the local host is arm64 under Docker Desktop's linuxkit VM, so its 12 cores flatter parallel scenarios and the disk is virtualised. The Fly box is the single-fractional-core reality of the cheapest deploy. Disk write-bytes are measured via /proc/self/io on both; absolute disk latency is not the point here — relative write amplification and the memory/file behaviour are, and those match across platforms.

How to reproduce

# local — builds the bench image, runs the matrix on the container's own fs
BENCH_DUR=3s ./test/bench/run-bench.sh          # → test/bench/out/results.json

# opt-in queue create/send/force-delete/converge churn
BENCH_ONLY=lifecycle_churn BENCH_DUR=2s ./test/bench/run-bench.sh

# hermetic HTTP-Hrana logical-lease trend (loopback; no Turso credentials)
go test ./engine -run '^$' -bench '^BenchmarkHranaSingleLeaseExec$' -benchmem -benchtime=3s

The historical Fly run used an environment-specific deployment file that is not part of this repository. Reproduce cloud measurements by deploying the committed test/bench/Dockerfile with your own explicit machine, region, volume and cleanup configuration, and record those inputs with the result.

Time-driven scenarios run for dur (3 seconds in the historical matrix); the fixed-volume drain and bloat scenarios instead run until their capped prefill is accounted for. Every scenario then enters an idle + GC + FreeOSMemory phase so we can measure what is reclaimed. A 200 ms background sampler records RSS + Go heap + DB/WAL file sizes throughout, and each scenario prints a [done] or [fail] line as it finishes (so a constrained box that stops early still leaves diagnostics for the scenarios already attempted).

The runner fails closed on workload operation errors: fixed-volume drains must match their exact prefill, mixed workloads reconcile accepted messages with completed plus remaining messages, and result-file failures produce a nonzero exit. For remote -db runs, use a dedicated non-production database. Each process uses a unique queue namespace, force-deletes only that namespace after every scenario, and drives bounded cleanup; an interrupted process can still leave its private namespace behind.

The opt-in lifecycle_churn scenario uses a fixed set of 64 queue names and never reuses a name until deletion has converged. Each cycle creates the queues, sends small batches, accepts forced deletion, and runs bounded maintenance until every name is absent. Four queues carry 1,024 messages so the test covers pending cleanup; the other 60 carry 16 messages. The live message-body payload stays below 1 MiB. Its result reports immediate and pending acknowledgements, maintenance passes, convergence latency, peak payload, and DB/WAL size. Here ops/s means fully converged queue lifecycles per second; the generic latency columns measure the initial delete acknowledgement.

A final 2-second native force-deletion smoke run on an Apple M1 Pro completed 640 queue lifecycles (10 cycles) at 289.17 lifecycles/s. All 640 deletions were accepted, 40 required background-style cleanup, convergence p99/max was 67.519/85.309 ms, and the database peaked at 5.528 MiB before ending at 0.480 MiB with a zero-byte WAL. This short run is a regression signal, not a deployment capacity claim; reproduce it on the target CPU, filesystem, durability mode, message sizes, and remote backend when applicable.

Native Go benchmarks cover topic fan-out, subscription create/empty-delete churn, and exact-total subscription pagination:

go test ./engine -run '^$' \
  -bench 'Benchmark(TopicFanout|SubscriptionCreateDelete|ListSubscriptionsPage)' \
  -benchmem -count=5

On an Apple M1 Pro with Go 1.26.9, the final recorded medians were 323.955 µs per create/delete lifecycle with 100 retained subscriptions and 328.866 µs with 10,000 retained subscriptions (1.015×). A 100-item page with an exact total measured 0.652 ms at 1,000 subscriptions and 5.168 ms at 10,000. A smoke with 5,000 queued messages acknowledged force deletion in 3.203 ms and converged in one 29.367 ms maintenance pass. These control-plane measurements found no strong lifecycle regression, but the exact count scales with inventory; do not treat the 10,000-subscription safety ceiling as a low-latency guarantee.

The native suite also covers fixed-lifetime fan-out and indexed subscription-expiry passes:

go test ./engine -run '^$' \
  -bench 'Benchmark(TopicFanoutTTL32|SubscriptionExpiry)' \
  -benchmem -count=5

On the same Apple M1 Pro with Go 1.26.9, seven alternating one-second rounds compared the fixed-lifetime implementation with the same suite before TTL support. Median latency changed by +2.50% for SendOne, -0.43% for SendBatch64, -3.32% for 32-way topic fan-out, -0.45% for 256-way fan-out, and +0.86% for receive plus complete. All remained below the 10% investigation threshold. In a separate same-binary comparison, 32-way fixed-lifetime fan-out had a 1.512 ms median, 3.62% above permanent subscriptions by independent medians; it added 32 allocations and 255 bytes per publish. Shared-host variation means neither the small gains nor this small cost is an optimization or SLA claim.

An indexed expiry scan over 10,000 future deadlines took 56.808 µs per no-work pass (17,603 passes/s). Transitioning a full 1,000-subscription due batch took 3.306 ms (302,459 subscriptions/s). A controlled burst created 10,000 subscriptions with one 5,000-message backlog, then advanced them to one common deadline. Data-plane fencing was immediate; 19 manually driven bounded passes discarded the backlog and removed all metadata in 338 ms. With normal background workers, 10,000 empty subscriptions converged in 1.292 s. A permanent queue had no send errors during cleanup; its send p50 stayed near 0.1 ms, while p99 rose from 0.687 ms before expiry to 12.003 ms during the burst (34.499 ms maximum). This is the expected bounded tail-latency cost of many simultaneous expirations, not a capacity promise; stagger deadlines and load-test the target backend.

Adding required lifecycle timestamps to 100-item subscription pages changed the 1,000-item inventory median from 0.658 ms to 0.712 ms (+8.21%) and the 10,000-item median from 5.187 ms to 5.325 ms (+2.66%). Page memory fell from about 39 KB to 30 KB after exact preallocation; allocation counts stayed effectively flat.

Observation cost under a deep current backlog

The native observation benchmarks use 300 queues with 300,000 messages retained at the same time. This is current backlog, not cumulative broker throughput: completed messages normally leave the table when settled. Run the committed fixtures with:

go test ./engine -run '^$' \
  -bench 'Benchmark(ObservationDeepBacklog|SendDuringDeepObservation)$' \
  -benchmem -count=3

Per-queue Stats uses state-specific indexes. Global Observe must still scan the retained rows when its roughly 10-second shared cache needs a refresh; cache hits still allocate and serialize the full queue response. The deliberately hostile continuous_observe benchmark calls observation as fast as possible and is a stress case, not a recommended scrape interval.

The final aggregate query replaced per-state SUM expressions with selective COUNT ... FILTER aggregates while keeping one grouped scan. On an Apple M1 Pro with Go 1.26.9, three measured refreshes in each of three runs produced:

Current retained distribution Earlier SUM median Current FILTER median Median change
300,000 active 248.369 ms 210.754 ms -15.14%
50,000 in each of six states 244.973 ms 210.518 ms -14.06%

This isolates aggregate-expression cost; it is not a deployment capacity result. The refresh remains proportional to retained rows and competes for CPU, page cache, storage bandwidth, and WAL checkpoint headroom even though a local file uses a separate read-only observation connection.

A five-pair local-file pressure run compared baseline and monitored 20-second phases at 1,000 scheduled sends/s. Each monitored phase made the expected global refreshes and per-queue calls; every admitted message completed and each phase ended with zero backlog. The preselected paired-median 10% investigation threshold failed for every foreground p99 measure:

Measure Paired-median monitored change
Throughput -1.06%
Dropped offered slots +1.05 percentage points
Send p99 +18.50%
Receive p99 +14.80%
Complete p99 +53.03%
End-to-end p99 +154.12%

Host variation was material and individual pairs moved in both directions, so the run supports stable throughput and completed-work accounting at that offered load. It does not show that monitoring has no foreground tail-latency cost. A separate 500 sends/s run also contained one severe adverse window, so it did not establish a tail-latency-safe operating point.

Monitored WAL peaks were 4.32–5.34 times their paired baselines in the 1,000/s run. After each phase, a passive checkpoint reported no busy reader and all frames checkpointed; a following truncating checkpoint left a zero-byte WAL. Observation can therefore cause transient WAL growth even when the file is reclaimable after the reader finishes. Start production scraping at 15 seconds, then measure refresh duration, WAL growth, and foreground p99 with the target backlog and hardware.

Remote Turso trend soak

The manually dispatched Turso performance soak Action exercises one package-internal Engine directly against the dedicated verification database. It is separate from the HTTP broker and uses four closed-loop lanes: two standard queues, one group_fifo queue and one strict_fifo queue. Each lane repeatedly sends one unique 256-byte body, receives and verifies that exact body, then completes it before starting the next cycle. This keeps the live message working set bounded while exercising normal background maintenance.

The four logical lanes share a fixed admission limit of one harness database call in flight (foreground_max_in_flight=1 in metadata.json). Their initial starts use nominal 0, 250, 500 and 750 ms offsets, recorded as a 250 ms lane-start stagger in the metadata. Against the four-connection remote pool, this avoids a synchronized startup burst and keeps foreground call demand below the pool limit, providing headroom for normal background maintenance. The profile is deliberately a sustainable stability and trend load. It is not a capacity test, and its throughput must not be read as the backend's maximum.

The admission limit applies only to calls made by the harness. Engine background workers bypass it, and it does not reserve the Turso primary's serialized write lock.

Choose 2, 10 or 30 minutes when dispatching the workflow. Start with 2 minutes to verify credentials, cleanup and evidence collection; use 30 minutes for the intended sustained trend check. The workflow and the existing Turso nightly suite share one repository-wide concurrency lock because both use TestMain to reset the same database. Both workflows have a fail-closed allowlist for the verification host before tests can reset it. Never point either workflow at a production database.

Each minute, and once more for a final partial window, the artifact records per-lane and overall cycles/s; Send, Receive, Complete and end-to-end p50/p95/p99 and maximum latency; empty/error counts; queue backlog; settlement-receipt counts; storage outcomes and retries; pool waits; background-maintenance pass state; Go heap, RSS, goroutines, GC and process CPU where the runner exposes them. The maintenance snapshot is copied from process memory and does not issue an additional remote database query. metadata.json, windows.jsonl, summary.json, summary.md and the test log are retained for 14 days. Errors, body mismatches, accounting failures, final backlog or exact cleanup failures fail the run, while the evidence written before a failure remains uploadable. Foreground failures and per-window storage errors include the safe generated category, HTTP/SQLite status where available, and a one-way error fingerprint. Provider text, URLs, credentials and message bodies are never copied into this evidence; the fingerprint is only a correlation key for private logs.

A single non-final Stats or settlement-receipt-count sample that fails with the connection category is recorded as a gap and may recover at the next scheduled sample; the harness does not issue an extra query to force recovery. During that gap, the overall and per-lane backlog and settlement-receipt fields are null, and older values are not presented as final state. A second monitoring failure anywhere in the run, any other operation or error category (including a working-set invariant), or a failed final sample fails the soak. Each window records structured monitoring status, and the summary records the failed-sample count and recovery status.

A single failed maintenance pass may recover on that task's next complete pass. Two consecutive failed passes, or one still unrecovered at the end of the run, fail the soak. Recovered failures remain visible in the cumulative maintenance counters and bounded diagnostic history. The final maintenance judgement is a process-memory snapshot taken after Engine.Close has stopped and joined the background workers; the harness does not trigger an extra maintenance pass to change the result. Thus the last windows.jsonl entry is the pre-cleanup workload sample, while summary.json.final_maintenance is the post-close terminal state. A runner cancellation or outer test timeout can interrupt final cleanup; the next run's TestMain reset and namespaced startup cleanup remove that residue.

The first-to-last window change is descriptive and has no performance threshold because GitHub-hosted runner placement, shared CPU and network path add noise. Turso does not expose physical database or WAL file sizes through this client; those JSON fields are null, never a misleading zero. Settlement receipts have 30-minute retention, so a 30-minute run's final receipt count is a current retention snapshot rather than a lifetime completion total.

1 · Throughput & write amplification

256 B bodies unless noted. wB/op = bytes physically written to disk per op (write amplification). The local box is 12 fast cores; the cloud box is one fraction of a throttled core — read the two columns as "engine character" vs "cheapest real box".

scenario sync local ops/s cloud ops/s local wB/op cloud wB/op
produce_p1 NORMAL 15,926 4,000 9,740 9,696
produce_p4 NORMAL 17,449 567 9,744 9,667
produce_p8 NORMAL 17,963 322 9,745 9,635
batch_16_p4 NORMAL 30,748 1,600 1,979 1,928
batch_64_p4 NORMAL 35,146 6,000 1,090 1,045
e2e_4x4 NORMAL 4,413 197 58,539 55,809
sessions_64g NORMAL 3,789 164 71,016 67,794
produce_p4_FULL FULL 1,556 468 13,743 13,682
props_p4 NORMAL 15,909 1,000 10,577 10,493
props_batch64 NORMAL 24,161 6,700 1,641 1,622

Write amplification was similar in these two runs — every cloud wB/op is within 5% of its local counterpart. The samples suggest that SQLite + WAL dominate this cost (a 256 B message was about 9.7 KB written singly and 1.1 KB batched), but two environments do not establish a platform-independent constant. Measure the target filesystem and workload before capacity planning.

On a single fractional core, concurrency hurts — produce_p1 4.0k > produce_p4 567 > produce_p8 322. With GOMAXPROCS=1 there's no parallelism to exploit, so more producers just add lock contention + scheduler/GC thrash on the one writer. On the cheap box the right pattern is one producer that batches, not many concurrent single-sends.

Batching is the great equaliser — batch_64 does 6.0k/s on the same throttled core that only manages 567/s of single produce_p4 (≈10×), at ~1/9 the write amplification. Enriched batched sends (props_batch64) hold 6.7k/s.

FULL durability costs ~11× locally; on the already-CPU-bound cloud box the gap narrows (468 vs 567) because fsync isn't the bottleneck there — the core is.

2 · Memory footprint after a short idle

Whole-process RSS (not just Go heap), peak during load vs after the harness's short 1.9-second idle and forced GC. This end snapshot describes immediate process state; it does not imply that the 60-second storage janitor has run.

scenario local peak → short idle cloud peak → short idle
produce_p8 34 → 27 MB 27 → 20 MB
batch_64_p4 32 → 27 MB 28 → 23 MB
props_batch64 33 → 29 MB 29 → 25 MB
size_16KB 33 → 29 MB 27 → 23 MB
drain_4c (200k msgs) 33 → 28 MB — (see §7)

Peak RSS was 27–34 MB across the scenarios listed above. The local 200k-message drain and 16 KB body scenarios stayed within that measured range. SQLite stores the backlog on disk, but this does not bound all broker memory. RSS declined after load stopped; no sustained growth was observed in these runs. Larger messages, more concurrent requests or queues, and monitoring can change the footprint. Measure the current workload before choosing a memory limit.

3 · DB-file footprint and reclamation

bloat_50k now inserts exactly 50,000 messages once, samples the full backlog, drains exactly that count with Complete, and rejects any send, receive, settle, or accounting error. file_bytes_per_msg uses the count actually accepted during prefill. Older results from this scenario are not comparable: the previous harness prefilled twice, rounded each tail batch up, and still divided file size by 50,000.

The scenario's db_final_mb is the immediate state after the same 1.9-second idle used by the other scenarios. It is useful for comparing the peak with the drained file, but it does not verify background page reclamation. Local file databases use auto_vacuum=INCREMENTAL; the background janitor checks every 60 seconds and reclaims a bounded number of pages once its freelist threshold is met. Use a run that spans that interval, or measure an explicit Compact(false), when evaluating reclamation. Remote Turso manages its own storage.

4 · Enriched messages — KV properties

props_* send a realistic message: a Properties map (tenant / trace_id / event_type / priority / source / schema_ver) plus CorrelationID, Subject, ContentType — "normal usage", vs a bare body.

scenario local ops/s fileB/msg vs bare
produce_p4 (bare) 17,449 415 —
props_p4 15,909 693 +280 B/msg on disk, ~9 % slower
batch_64_p4 (bare) 35,146 373 —
props_batch64 24,161 664 +291 B/msg, ~31 % slower batched

Properties are cheap on a single send (9 % throughput, +280 B/msg) but cost more when batched (31 %): once commit overhead is amortised away, the per-message JSON-encode of the KV map becomes the dominant work.

5 · Body-size sweep

4 producers, NORMAL, body 64 B → 16 KB:

body local ops/s cloud ops/s wB/op (≈both) fileB/msg
64 B 17,205 1,200 9,122 217
256 B 17,449 567 9,744 415
1 KB 13,991 912 12,980 1,489
4 KB 12,547 454 22,205 4,740
16 KB 7,988 259 46,939 17,091

On-disk storage was roughly linear with body size in this sweep. The measured difference between body size and fileB/msg ranged from 153 to 707 bytes, so the table does not support one fixed row/index-overhead constant. Throughput was commit-bound up to about 256 B and then increasingly byte-bound. Default body cap is 1 MiB (MaxMessageBytes).

6 · Load ramp & consumer churn (local)

  • rampdown_4x4: produce hard, then stop producing while consumers drain to idle. RSS peak 31 MB → 27 MB after the load goes away — memory tracks the workload down, not a one-way ratchet.
  • churn_consumers: producers steady while consumer cohorts repeatedly go online/offline. RSS stays ~28–34 MB across cycles with no stair-step growth — connect/disconnect doesn't leak.

7 · Cloud reality — what a 256 MB fractional core changes

The Fly shared-cpu-1x is GOMAXPROCS=1 with CPU-steal. Versus the 12-core local box:

  1. Memory stayed low in the measured scenarios. Peak RSS was 27–29 MB for the cloud scenarios in §2, with reclamation after load. This does not establish the memory required by other workloads or current releases.
  2. Write amplification was close in these two runs. Cloud values were within 5% of local; validate that relationship on the target storage stack.
  3. Throughput: core-bound, and concurrency backfires. Single-send multi-producer collapses (567/s at p4, 322/s at p8) because there's no second core. Batch, and throughput recovers to thousands/s (6.0–6.7k).
  4. Tail latency: throttling shows up. p99 hits the 100 ms histogram ceiling on most multi-goroutine scenarios (CPU-steal stalls); single-producer scenarios keep p99 under ~5 ms.

In this short historical sample, batching reached about 6k msg/s on a shared-cpu-1x, while concurrent single sends reached only hundreds/s. These are workload observations, not a sustained-capacity or SLA claim.

Tuning knobs

mqlite ships sensible defaults; most deployments change nothing. In rough order of impact:

knob default when to change
batch size (messages:[…]) — the biggest lever — ~9× less write amplification, ~2× throughput. Batch whenever you can.
MQLITE_SYNC NORMAL FULL only if a power cut losing the last few commits is unacceptable; it costs ~11–18× on single sends, so pair it with batching.
wal_autocheckpoint 1000 pages (~4 MB) matched the no-long-reader historical baseline; observation snapshots and other readers can cause a larger transient WAL. Raise only after measuring the checkpoint and recovery trade-off.
cache_size ~2 MB the working set (queue heads + indexes) is small; raise only after profiling shows cache pressure under deep backlogs — it costs RAM on a 256 MB machine.
mmap_size off modernc.org/sqlite is pure-Go; don't assume C-SQLite mmap gains — measure first.
writer/provider pool local writer 1 / remote provider 4 don't change — the local writer pool stays at one for atomic claims; local files also have one read-only observation connection. The remote pool is scoped to one broker and Turso serializes commits. libsql:// logical connections are single-lease while the shared HTTP transport retains TCP/TLS reuse; see turso.md.

busy_timeout=5000 and temp_store=MEMORY are set on local modernc SQLite connections. They do not apply to remote Turso/libSQL connections, whose transient contention uses the bounded retry policy described in turso.md.

Findings summary

  1. Low measured memory with reclamation — peak RSS was 27–34 MB in the scenarios in §2. No sustained growth was observed during the recorded churn and ramp-down tests; validate the current workload separately.
  2. Batch to go fast — ~9× less write amplification, and on a single core the difference between hundreds/s and thousands/s.
  3. Write amplification was similar in two historical environments (~9.7 KB/op single, ~1.1 KB batched, with local/cloud pairs within 5%); it is not a universal platform constant.
  4. Single-writer model: more producers ≠ more write throughput; on one core they make it worse. Prefer one batching producer.
  5. Peak backlog is a primary sizing input. Add headroom for WAL, page/index overhead, fragmentation, reclamation lag, long readers and backups; background incremental_vacuum returns eligible free pages over time.
  6. NORMAL vs FULL is an ~11× durability dial (local); pick per host failure model.
  7. Properties are affordable; large bodies are byte-bound and storage-linear.

The historical source artifacts were captured in test/bench/out/results.json and the mqlite-bench Fly logs; they are not shipped in this repository. Treat the table as historical evidence and rerun the commands above before using the numbers for a current deployment decision.
